The brackets emphasize that a complex is a distinct chemical entity with its own properties. Within the brackets, the symbol of the central atom comes first. The electric charge on a coordination complex is the sum of the oxidation num­ ber of the metal ion and the charges of the ligands that surround it. Thus, the com­ plex of copper(II) (Cu21) with four Br2 ions is an anion with a 22 charge, [CuBr4]22.

Solution (a) The oxidation state of K is known to be 11, so the complex in brackets is an anion

with a 21 charge, [Co(NH3)2(CN)4]2. The charge on the two NH3 ligands is 0, and the charge on each of the four CN2 ligands is 21. The oxidation state of the Co must then be 13, because 4 × 21 (for the CN2) 1 2 × 0 (for the NH3) 1 3 (for Co) equals the required 21.
(b) The ligand CO has zero charge, and the complex has zero charge as well. Therefore,
the oxidation state of the osmium is 0.
(c) There are three neutral ligands (the water mol­e­cules) and three ligands with 21
charges (the hydroxide ions). The Na1 ion contributes only 11; thus, the oxidation state of the cobalt must be 12.

Coordination modifies the chemical and physical properties of both the central atom and the ligands. Consider the chemistry of aqueous cyanide (CN2) and iron(II) (Fe21) ions. The CN2 ion reacts immediately with acid to generate gaseous HCN, a deadly poison, and Fe21, when mixed with aqueous base, instantly precipi­ tates a gelatinous hydroxide. The reaction between Fe21 and CN2 produces the complex ion [Fe(CN)6]42(aq), which undergoes n­either of the two reactions just described nor any others considered characteristic of CN2 or Fe21. Ions or mol­e­ cules may be pre­sent in multiple forms in the same compound. The two Cl2 ions in [Pt(NH3)3Cl]Cl are chemically different, because one is coordinated and the other is not. Treatment of an aqueous solution of this substance with Ag1 immediately precipitates the uncoordinated Cl2 as AgCl(s), but not the coordinated Cl2, just as it did for Werner’s complexes discussed earlier.

Ionic coordination complexes of opposite charges can combine with each other—just as any positive ion can combine with a negative ion—to form salts.
